workload.problem: damped harmonic oscillator x'' + 2 zeta omega x' + omega^2 x = 0, classical RK4, fixed step (perf_card.py)
workload.counting_rule: Useful FLOPs = 44 per running sample per step: the add, subtract and multiply operations of the hawk-emitted step (negation not counted), times the number of (sample, step) pairs that are still running. The same count is used for every arm, so FLOP/s compares useful work.

method.warm_up: one run per arm and cell, excluded; it is also the verification run
method.interleaving: the arm order rotates by one every repetition
method.settle: 0.2 s pause before every timed repetition, so the previous arm's thread pools stop spin-waiting first, then 0.05 s of untimed runs of the arm itself, so the timed block starts on a ramped clock (the machine's busy cores during the pause and the clock at the timer start are recorded per row)
method.inner_runs: a repetition whose run is shorter than 0.1 s repeats it back to back until the repetition spans at least 0.1 s (count fixed per arm and cell from a 0.05 s calibration block of back-to-back runs after the ramp, at most 2000; recorded per row as inner_runs) and records the mean per run; eagle's untimed input copy runs between the repeats
method.isolation: every arm runs in its own persistent worker process with its thread pools pinned by environment and API; only one arm runs at a time
method.wall: the integration alone, inputs already in the arm's own arrays or tensors (eagle: copied into its bound arrays before the timer; multiprocessing: chunk transfer to and from the pool is inside the timer; plain Python: list conversion inside)
method.cpu_busy: process CPU seconds (getrusage, plus pool processes) / wall
method.compile: eagle: eagle.deploy of the host kernel, plain or active-set (the hawk compile cache may serve it); Numba: first call on a tiny batch; JAX: lower + compile per N from abstract shapes; multiprocessing: pool start-up; NumPy, PyTorch, Python: none
method.verification: all arms reach identical per-sample step counts; x and v agree with eagle_term8 within absolute 1e-11
method.load_avg_1m: per_cell rows already carry load_avg_before/after (os.getloadavg()); eagle_term8/eagle_term1 and eagle_compact8/eagle_compact1/eagle_reorder8/eagle_reorder1 are the 1-thread vs N-thread rows
method.slot_fill: n/a on the host (device-only hook; see perf_card.py)
method.nsys_counts: n/a on the host (no nsys trace here)
method.fixed_overhead: not re-measured as a dedicated cell on this card; per_cell's inner_runs/wall already show per-call overhead shrinking at small N

summary: eagle's host build of the step (hawk host profile `native`: -O3 -ffp-contract=off -mcpu=native -std=c++23 -shared -fPIC -DAETHER_CPP_MODE, no -march) is not vectorised: its entry function holds scalar float64 instructions (none) and packed ones (none); the 8-thread speed-up over 1 thread comes from the OpenMP team.
The active-set build of the step (compaction and reorder arms) is not vectorised (packed float64 instructions: none).
Numba's compiled loop uses scalar float64 instructions only (each sample's steps are a dependent chain).
NumPy and PyTorch use their libraries' own SIMD kernels for each array operation; JAX's XLA code was not inspected.

compile_time.method: Its own pass, never part of any wall. Each measurement is a fresh process: the imports run untimed, then the timer spans the first call to a ready kernel (trace + code generation + compile, or the cache lookup). Cold: an empty cache (hawk's compile cache pointed at a fresh directory through HAWK_CACHE_DIR; Numba with cache=True into a fresh NUMBA_CACHE_DIR; JAX with its persistent compilation cache in a fresh directory). Warm: a new process on the cache the first cold run populated (hawk cache hit; Numba's on-disk cache; JAX's persistent cache with the minimum compile time and entry size set to 0). hawk: eagle.deploy of the kernel (tracing, C++ emission, the g++ host build, eagle's plan); the active-set variant is a second build of the same step. Numba: the first call on a 64-sample batch (compile plus a negligible run). JAX: lower + compile from abstract shapes, once per N (XLA specialises on the shape). Medians of 3 cold and 3 warm processes.

memory.method: A separate pass after the timing pass. Each (arm, N, configuration) runs in a fresh process: imports, then a warm-up run on a 64-sample batch (every JIT compiles here; JAX also compiles for shape N from abstract shapes), then the baseline (resident set size, VmRSS) and a reset of the process's peak mark (/proc/self/clear_refs, so ru_maxrss restarts from the baseline); then the batch's inputs are generated and one full run done. Peak memory = ru_maxrss at the end minus the baseline; for multiprocessing, plus each pool process's own peak above its baseline (shared pages counted once per process). Minimum = the state the workload needs, N × ((2 state + 2 float64 scalars: omega, zeta) × 8 + 4 bytes for the stop step as a 32-bit integer) = 36 bytes per sample; the factor is peak / minimum. Compile overhead = baseline minus the resident size before the arm's imports-and-warm-up. Below about 1 MiB the allocator reuses memory already resident at the baseline, so small-N peaks can read below the minimum.

fit.intro: Each tool below is written the way its users write it. Two loop structures appear: per step over the batch (eagle's termination loops, JAX, PyTorch, NumPy, multiprocessing) and per sample over its steps (Numba, plain Python). The per-sample structure touches each sample's state once for all its steps; the per-step structure streams the batch through memory every step, which is the structure the GPU card's kernels use. Ratios below are wall-time ratios at the largest N each arm ran (below 1 = less time than eagle at 8 threads).

arms.eagle_term8: The GPU card's eagle graph arm, unchanged, on the host: the same hawk step kernel, eagle.deploy and eagle.until_done call, run by eagle's OpenMP host team; one code base for GPUs and CPUs. On this card: spread S=100, N=1,000,000: 34.6 ms; spread S=1000, N=1,000,000: 330 ms; uniform S=1000, N=1,000,000: 648 ms. Fastest in 7 of 12 cells.
arms.eagle_term1: The same loop on one thread: the difference to the 8-thread row is the threading alone. On this card: spread S=100, N=1,000,000: 275 ms (7.96× eagle 8-thread time); spread S=1000, N=1,000,000: 2.64 s (7.98× eagle 8-thread time); uniform S=1000, N=1,000,000: 5.17 s (7.98× eagle 8-thread time). Fastest in 0 of 12 cells.
arms.eagle_compact8: The GPU card's compaction arm on the host: the launch covers only the samples still running, the map rebuilt every 16 steps when a sample finished. On this card: spread S=100, N=1,000,000: 52.1 ms (1.51× eagle 8-thread time); spread S=1000, N=1,000,000: 301 ms (0.91× eagle 8-thread time); uniform S=1000, N=1,000,000: 957 ms (1.48× eagle 8-thread time). Fastest in 1 of 12 cells.
arms.eagle_compact1: The compaction loop on one thread: the difference to the 8-thread row is the threading alone. On this card: spread S=100, N=1,000,000: 208 ms (6.02× eagle 8-thread time); spread S=1000, N=1,000,000: 1.76 s (5.32× eagle 8-thread time); uniform S=1000, N=1,000,000: 7.25 s (11.2× eagle 8-thread time). Fastest in 0 of 12 cells.
arms.eagle_reorder8: The GPU card's reorder arm on the host: the live samples moved to the front of every plane when they spread thin, restored to sample order at the end (inside the wall). On this card: spread S=100, N=1,000,000: 131 ms (3.79× eagle 8-thread time); spread S=1000, N=1,000,000: 397 ms (1.2× eagle 8-thread time); uniform S=1000, N=1,000,000: 953 ms (1.47× eagle 8-thread time). Fastest in 0 of 12 cells.
arms.eagle_reorder1: The reorder loop on one thread: the difference to the 8-thread row is the threading alone. On this card: spread S=100, N=1,000,000: 274 ms (7.92× eagle 8-thread time); spread S=1000, N=1,000,000: 1.72 s (5.2× eagle 8-thread time); uniform S=1000, N=1,000,000: 7.26 s (11.2× eagle 8-thread time). Fastest in 0 of 12 cells.
arms.numba_prange: Compiles a plain Python loop to machine code with no separate language; each sample keeps its state in registers across all of its steps and stops on its own, so finished samples cost nothing. On this card: spread S=100, N=1,000,000: 39 ms (1.13× eagle 8-thread time); spread S=1000, N=1,000,000: 388 ms (1.17× eagle 8-thread time); uniform S=1000, N=1,000,000: 1.8 s (2.78× eagle 8-thread time). Fastest in 1 of 12 cells.
arms.jax_shard8: The JAX arm spread over 8 CPU devices: the batch is sharded and each shard runs its own vmapped while loop, with no cross-shard step synchronisation. On this card: spread S=100, N=1,000,000: 42.6 ms (1.23× eagle 8-thread time); spread S=1000, N=1,000,000: 410 ms (1.24× eagle 8-thread time); uniform S=1000, N=1,000,000: 411 ms (0.635× eagle 8-thread time). Fastest in 3 of 12 cells.
arms.jax_vmap: Compiles the whole loop once and batches a per-sample while loop with vmap; the same code runs on GPUs and differentiates with jax.grad. On this card: spread S=100, N=1,000,000: 185 ms (5.35× eagle 8-thread time); spread S=1000, N=1,000,000: 1.77 s (5.34× eagle 8-thread time); uniform S=1000, N=1,000,000: 1.76 s (2.72× eagle 8-thread time). Fastest in 0 of 12 cells.
arms.torch_masked: Runs the masked array version on a multi-threaded tensor library; it fits where the computation already lives next to a PyTorch model or needs autograd. On this card: spread S=100, N=1,000,000: 304 ms (8.79× eagle 8-thread time); spread S=1000, N=1,000,000: 3.02 s (9.15× eagle 8-thread time); uniform S=1000, N=1,000,000: 2.76 s (4.26× eagle 8-thread time). Fastest in 0 of 12 cells.
arms.numpy_masked: No compile step and no dependency beyond NumPy; masked array code computes every sample every step, so it fits dense batches where all samples run to the end (the uniform configuration). On this card: spread S=100, N=1,000,000: 1.59 s (46× eagle 8-thread time); spread S=1000, N=1,000,000: 16.4 s (49.5× eagle 8-thread time); uniform S=1000, N=1,000,000: 15.6 s (24× eagle 8-thread time). Fastest in 0 of 12 cells.
arms.mp_numpy: Spreads NumPy over processes with the standard library alone; each chunk stops once its own samples are done. On this card: spread S=100, N=1,000,000: 244 ms (7.05× eagle 8-thread time); spread S=1000, N=1,000,000: 2.22 s (6.72× eagle 8-thread time); uniform S=1000, N=1,000,000: 2.2 s (3.4× eagle 8-thread time). Fastest in 0 of 12 cells.
arms.python_loops: Nothing to install and each line can be stepped in a debugger; run only at small N here. On this card: spread S=100, N=10,000: 60.5 ms (158× eagle 8-thread time); spread S=1000, N=10,000: 580 ms (166× eagle 8-thread time); uniform S=1000, N=1,000: 266 ms (381× eagle 8-thread time). Fastest in 0 of 12 cells.
